scenes.text: Chapter one. The cave.
scenes.query: Tham Luang cave system map diagram

scenes.text: June twenty-third, twenty eighteen. Chiang Rai, northern Thailand. Twelve boys from the Wild Boars youth football club, ages eleven to sixteen, walk into Tham Luang cave with their assistant coach after practice.
Coach Ekkapol Chantawong is twenty-five. He was orphaned as a child, spent years as a novice Buddhist monk, and is legally stateless, along with at least three of the boys on this team.

scenes.cap: Ekkapol Chantawong. Stateless. A former monk.

scenes.text: Unseasonal monsoon rain floods the cave's lower passages while they're inside, cutting off the exit and pushing the group deeper. That evening, the head coach, a different man named Nopparat, finds twenty missed calls from parents.
Thai Navy Seal divers reach a chamber called Pattaya Beach two days later, and turn back. The water beyond it has never been mapped.

scenes.text: Cave diving is not scuba diving. In zero visibility, in a current, a diver has to feel the walls with both hands, laying a guide line as they go, because turning around and simply swimming back is not always possible.

scenes.text: That is why this call went out not to the Thai military alone, but to a small, specific community of civilian cave-diving experts scattered across Britain, Australia, Belgium, and beyond.
June twenty-ninth. Thailand's Prime Minister visits the site in person, and asks publicly that the country stay focused on the rescue, not on blaming a coach for taking children into a cave.

scenes.text: Chapter two. Thirteen days, and a country's worth of water.
scenes.chapter:
CHAPTER TWO
A COUNTRY'S WORTH OF WATER

scenes.text: Within a week, the operation scales past six hundred people, then past ten thousand: engineers, soldiers, and volunteers from seventeen countries.

Over a hundred farmers watch roughly fifty-five hundred acres of their own rice fields deliberately flooded, diverted on purpose to slow water pouring into the mountain. It is barely mentioned in any film made about this rescue.
scenes.cap: 5,500 acres of farmland, flooded on purpose.

scenes.text: More than one billion litres of water are pumped out of the mountain, roughly four hundred Olympic swimming pools, while engineers drill over a hundred boreholes from the surface hunting for a shaft that never finds them.
Officials debate teaching the boys to dive out themselves. Rejected: they are untrained children in a technical cave system that has already turned back Navy SEALs.
scenes.query: cave diving technical equipment dark water

scenes.text: Waiting out the roughly four-month monsoon season with food ferried in was the safest plan on paper. It was rejected too: dwindling oxygen, rising water, and thirteen people who could not simply wait that long.

By July fourth, pumps are removing water at a peak rate of one point six million litres an hour. Engineers will end up drilling past a hundred boreholes into the mountain, searching for a shaft that never once finds the group.
Chapter three. The Americans nobody put in the movie.
scenes.chapter:
CHAPTER THREE
NOBODY PUT THEM IN THE MOVIE

scenes.text: June twenty-eighth. A team from the 353rd Special Operations Group, U.S. Air Force, lands in Chiang Rai from Okinawa, Japan.

scenes.text: The technique itself, moving a person hand-to-hand through a passage too narrow to swim through side by side, was later demonstrated using a training dummy at a US base in Japan, for exactly this reason: the real thing happened in total darkness, with no camera able to survive the trip.

scenes.text: British divers Jason Mallinson and Chris Jewell joined the extraction team as well, alongside Volanthen and Stanton. By the final count, thirteen international cave divers and five Thai Navy SEALs made up the extraction team.
Chapter four. Found.

July second, evening. Nine days in. British divers John Volanthen and Rick Stanton, laying line two and a half kilometers into the flooded system, surface at a mud slope and find all thirteen of them alive.

scenes.text: Nine days with almost no food. All thirteen conscious, coherent, and alive. It is, to this day, one of the only rescues of its kind in recorded history to end this way.

scenes.text: Australian anaesthetist Richard Harris and his diving partner, veterinarian Craig Challen, are flown in specifically for what comes next. Harris will end up making the single riskiest call of the entire operation.
Chapter five. The billionaire's submarine.
July eighth. Elon Musk tweets that a child-sized submersible, built from a spare Falcon 9 rocket part, is on its way to help.
Two days later, the rescue is completed without it. The operation's on-site commander, Narongsak Osatanakorn, calls the device impractical for the cave's narrow, twisting passages.
The device itself, nicknamed "Wild Boar" after the trapped team, was built by SpaceX and Boring Company engineers out of a spare Falcon 9 rocket part, and actually flown to the site.

On July thirteenth, British caver Vernon Unsworth, who had lived locally and helped coordinate the rescue, tells CNN the submarine was a "PR stunt," and that Musk should, in his words, "stick his submarine where it hurts."
scenes.cap: "A PR stunt." — Vernon Unsworth, CNN, July 13, 2018.

scenes.text: Two days after that, Musk fires back on Twitter: "Sorry pedo guy, you really did ask for it." He deletes it and apologizes within days.
Chapter six. The trial nobody filmed.
scenes.chapter:
CHAPTER SIX
THE TRIAL NOBODY FILMED

scenes.text: Unsworth sues for defamation that September, seeking one hundred ninety million dollars. In private emails to a reporter, Musk goes further, calling Unsworth a child rapist, with no evidence.
Musk goes further still, in a private email exchange with a reporter, calling Unsworth a "child rapist" and claiming, with no evidence at all, that he had moved to Thailand for a child bride.
scenes.cap: Unproven. Never adjudicated true or false by any court.

scenes.text: The reporter had not agreed to keep any of it off the record. He published the emails in full.
A judge rules Unsworth a private citizen, not a public figure, for these statements, meaning Musk would only need to have acted carelessly, not maliciously, to lose.

That single ruling matters more than it sounds: a public figure has to prove a defendant knew a statement was false, or recklessly ignored the truth. A private citizen only has to prove ordinary carelessness. The bar for Unsworth to win had just gotten lower.
December third, twenty nineteen. A four-day jury trial in Los Angeles. Musk testifies. He apologizes to Unsworth on the stand and says no one actually understood the tweet to mean pedophile.

Musk's defense, laid out at trial: that "pedo guy" was old South African slang for a creepy old man, not a literal accusation, and that the tweet, which never actually named Unsworth, couldn't reasonably be read as being about him specifically.

Unsworth's team sought one hundred ninety million dollars in damages, pointing to Musk's roughly twenty billion dollar net worth at the time. The judge instructed the jury the private emails could describe Musk's state of mind, but could not, on their own, prove defamation.
The jury deliberates for under an hour. They find Musk not liable. Zero damages. A civil verdict, not a criminal one.

By one juror's own account afterward, the panel never even reached the question of whether the accusation was true. They simply weren't convinced a reasonable person could tell an un-named tweet was about Unsworth at all.
scenes.cap: The jury never ruled on whether it was true.

scenes.text: Chapter seven. The extraction nobody could have filmed.
scenes.chapter:
CHAPTER SEVEN
NOBODY COULD HAVE FILMED THIS

scenes.text: Oxygen inside the boys' chamber falls toward fifteen percent, well below breathable. Officials abandon every plan except one: sedate all thirteen, and carry them out through the flooded cave, one at a time.
Every other option had already failed or been rejected. This was the last plan left on the table, and nobody involved was certain it would work on a single child, let alone all thirteen.

The real drug protocol, published later in the New England Journal of Medicine by the operation's own medical team: an anti-anxiety tablet, atropine, then a ketamine injection, chosen specifically because it doesn't suppress breathing.

Ketamine specifically, because unlike almost every other sedative available, it doesn't suppress the drive to keep breathing, something that mattered enormously for a swim that would last hours through cold water.
Each boy is fitted with a full-face oxygen mask and physically carried through the flooded passages by a lead diver, sedated the entire way.
scenes.cap: RECONSTRUCTION — the only real footage of this sequence is Thai government-produced and was never released under a free license.

scenes.text: The order they came out in wasn't decided by the doctors. The boys decided it themselves, days earlier, trapped in the dark: whoever lived farthest from the cave should go first, so they wouldn't have as far to bike home.
scenes.cap: "So the persons who live furthest away would go out first." — Ekkapol Chantawong.

scenes.text: July sixth. Thai Navy Seal volunteer Saman Kunan runs out of his own air returning from delivering oxygen tanks, and dies. He is posthumously promoted seven ranks by royal command.
scenes.cap: Saman Kunan, 37. July 6, 2018. RECONSTRUCTION — no footage exists.

scenes.text: Eighteen months later, a second Seal, Petty Officer Beirut Pakbara, dies from a blood infection contracted during the same mission. Almost no retelling of this story mentions his name at all.
scenes.cap: Beirut Pakbara. Died Dec 28, 2019. Rarely mentioned.

scenes.text: Two deaths, on two completely different timelines, both caused by the same eighteen-day mission. Most retellings only remember one of them.

July tenth. Eighteen divers, thirteen from around the world and five Thai Navy SEALs, bring out the last four boys, their coach, and the medical team who never left their side. Eighteen days after they walked in, everyone is out.
By the third and final day, what had taken roughly three hours per boy on day one had been cut to just over two. The team had gotten faster with every single life they carried out.
Chapter eight. What the story left out.
scenes.chapter:
CHAPTER EIGHT
WHAT THE STORY LEFT OUT

scenes.text: Freelance divers Ben Reymenants and Maksym Polejaka reportedly located the group first. The British divers every film credits didn't publicly acknowledge them for three years.
Not because their contribution was invented. Because the two men every screen adaptation lionizes hadn't been the ones to find them first, and that fact took years to become public.

Within weeks, Thailand fast-tracked citizenship for Ekkapol and the stateless boys on the team, members of the Tai Lue ethnic minority who had lived in Thailand their whole lives without ever legally belonging to it.

Ekkapol and the boys had lived their entire lives in Thailand, gone to Thai schools, spoken Thai, without ever holding the legal right to a Thai passport, a bank account, or in some cases, even to travel outside their home district.

Within days of the rescue, studios and streamers were racing to buy the rights to tell these boys' stories. Netflix's exclusive deal is the specific reason the Oscar-nominated documentary team never got to speak with them at all.

That auction is why the boys never appear at all in the Oscar-nominated documentary about their own rescue, and why the scripted Netflix series exists specifically because it, not the documentary team, held the rights to tell their side of it.

The documentary that did get real access, built from eighty-seven hours of footage the Thai Navy eventually handed over after two years of negotiation, went on to win a Bafta nomination and a string of Critics' Choice awards. It was still snubbed at the Oscars.
Chapter nine. Still diving, eight years later.
scenes.chapter:
CHAPTER NINE
STILL DIVING, EIGHT YEARS LATER

scenes.text: May twenty-nineteenth, twenty twenty-six. Eight villagers panning for gold enter a flooded mine in Xaysomboun Province, Laos. Monsoon rain traps seven of them underground.
Roughly a hundred rescuers respond, specialists from Thailand, Finland, France, Indonesia, Malaysia, Japan, and Australia.
Two of the divers who answer the call are Mikko Paasi and Norraseth Palasri, the same men who dove into Tham Luang in 2018.

scenes.cap: The same divers. Eight years later.

scenes.text: This time, it isn't a clean ending. Five survivors are found alive by May thirtieth. Two miners are never located. A cave-in and a real earthquake make the site too unstable, and on June sixth, officials call off the search.
scenes.cap: 2 of 7 never found. Search called off June 6, 2026.

scenes.text: One miner is pulled out in a high-risk underwater evacuation on May twenty-ninth. The last four walk out on their own the next day, once the water finally drops low enough.
A few weeks later, Chiang Rai holds its eighth anniversary memorial for the Tham Luang rescue: a tribute to Saman Kunan, to Beirut Pakbara, and to the boy who didn't live to see this anniversary.

Here is the part of this story that has nothing to do with mystery, and everything to do with the truth. In February twenty twenty-three, Duangphet Phromthep, the team's captain, one of the twelve boys who survived that cave, died in England. He was seventeen.

scenes.text: The coroner's own words, after a full inquest: he was not known to any mental health service, no one could have foreseen it, and there was no third-party involvement of any kind. The reason, in the coroner's own language, is simply not known.
scenes.cap: "It could not have been foreseen or prevented." — Coroner Catherine Mason.

scenes.text: Twelve boys and their coach walked into a cave in twenty eighteen. All thirteen walked out. What happened to them afterward, the trial, the citizenship, the divers still diving, the boy who didn't get to grow old, was never going to fit inside one clean, simple story.
If a rescue with a happy ending still had this much left unsaid, wait until you see the disaster where nothing about the ending was happy at all. That full story is live on this channel right now.
